claim: Centrioles are characterized by a nine-fold arrangement of microtubule triplets held together by an inner protein scaffold.
source: Centrioles are characterized by a nine-fold arrangement of microtubule triplets held together by an inner protein scaffold.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the structural organization of centrioles.

claim: POC16 and its human homolog WDR90 are components of the microtubule wall along the central core region of the centriole.
source: using ultrastructure expansion microscopy for nanoscale protein mapping, we reveal that POC16 and its human homolog WDR90 are components of the microtubule wall along the central core region of the centriole.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM experimental data showing the localization of POC16/WDR90.

claim: WDR90 is an evolutionary microtubule associated protein.
source: We further found that WDR90 is an evolutionary microtubule associated protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing microtubule binding across multiple species.

claim: WDR90 depletion impairs the localization of inner scaffold components.
source: we demonstrate that WDR90 depletion impairs the localization of inner scaffold components, leading to centriole structural abnormalities in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from siRNA depletion experiments.

claim: WDR90 depletion leads to centriole structural abnormalities in human cells.
source: we demonstrate that WDR90 depletion impairs the localization of inner scaffold components, leading to centriole structural abnormalities in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data showing structural defects.

claim: WDR90 is an evolutionary conserved molecular player participating in centriole architecture integrity.
source: Altogether, this work highlights that WDR90 is an evolutionary conserved molecular player participating in centriole architecture integrity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence across species.

claim: Defects in centriole assembly, size, structure and number lead to abnormal mitosis or defective ciliogenesis.
source: Consequently, defects in centriole assembly, size, structure and number lead to abnormal mitosis or defective ciliogenesis and have been associated with several human pathologies such as ciliopathies and cancer (Gönczy, 2015; Nigg and Holland, 2018; Nigg and Raff, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Centriole amplification can result from centriole fragmentation in defective, over-elongated centrioles.
source: For instance, centriole amplification, a hallmark of cancer cells, can result from centriole fragmentation in defective, over-elongated centrioles (Marteil et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marteil et al., 2018.

claim: Centrioles can be divided into three distinct regions termed proximal end, central core and distal tip.
source: Centrioles are characterized by a nine-fold radial arrangement of microtubule triplets, are polarized along their long axis, and can be divided in three distinct regions termed proximal end, central core and distal tip (Hamel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamel et al., 2017.

claim: The cartwheel on the proximal end is crucial for centriole assembly.
source: Each region displays specific structural features such as the cartwheel on the proximal end, which is crucial for centriole assembly (Nakazawa et al., 2007; Strnad et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakazawa et al., 2007 and Strnad et al., 2007.

claim: Distal appendages are essential for membrane docking during ciliogenesis.
source: or the distal appendages at the very distal region, essential for membrane docking during ciliogenesis (Tanos et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tanos et al., 2013.

claim: The inner centriole scaffold forms an extended helix covering ~70% of the centriole length.
source: Using cryo-tomography, we recently showed that the inner centriole scaffold forms an extended helix covering ~70% of the centriole length and that is rooted at the inner junction between the A and B microtubules (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-tomography data from the authors' previous work.

claim: The inner scaffold is rooted at the inner junction between the A and B microtubules.
source: Using cryo-tomography, we recently showed that the inner centriole scaffold forms an extended helix covering ~70% of the centriole length and that is rooted at the inner junction between the A and B microtubules (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-tomography data.

claim: The inner scaffold connection consists of a stem attaching the neighboring A and B microtubules and three arms extending from the same stem toward the centriolar lumen.
source: This connection consists of a stem attaching the neighboring A and B microtubules and three arms extending from the same stem toward the centriolar lumen (Le Guennec et al., 2020; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and Figure 1A,B showing the structure.

claim: The stem of the inner scaffold has been detected in Paramecium tetraurelia, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and human centrioles.
source: The stem of the inner scaffold has been detected in Paramecium tetraurelia, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and human centrioles, suggesting that it represents an evolutionary conserved structural feature.
evidence: This is supported by comparative structural data across species.

claim: POC16 localizes precisely on the microtubule wall in the central core region of Chlamydomonas centrioles.
source: From top viewed centrioles, we measured the distance between both POC16 and tubulin maximal intensity signal from the exterior to the interior of the centriole and found that POC16 localizes precisely on the microtubule wall in the central core region of Chlamydomonas centrioles (Figure 1M,N, average distance between POC16 and tubulin Δ = 0 nm +/- 8).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM measurements shown in Figure 1M,N.

claim: The endogenous POC16 longitudinal fluorescence signal is restricted to the central core region as compared to the tubulin signal in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii isolated centrioles.
source: We observed first in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii isolated centrioles that the endogenous POC16 longitudinal fluorescence signal is restricted to the central core region as compared to the tubulin signal, which depicts total centriolar length (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: POB15 localizes internally along the microtubule wall in Chlamydomonas centrioles with an average distance of 12 nm +/- 7 from tubulin.
source: As a control, we could recapitulate the internal localization along the microtubule wall of POB15, another central core protein (Figure 1G–I and Figure 1M,N, average distance between POB15 and tubulin Δ = 12 nm +/- 7) as previously reported using immunogold-labeling (Hamel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 1G-I and 1M,N, and confirmed by previous immunogold-labeling.

claim: WDR90 localizes on the centriolar microtubule wall in human centrioles with an average distance of 2 nm +/- 12 from tubulin.
source: We found that while WDR90 precisely localizes to the centriolar microtubule wall (Figure 1P, average distance between WDR90 and tubulin: Δ = 2 nm +/12)
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM measurements shown in Figure 1P.

claim: POC1B, FAM161A, POC5 and Centrin signals are shifted toward the centriole lumen in comparison to the tubulin signal.
source: POC1B, FAM161A, POC5 and Centrin signals were shifted toward the centriole lumen in comparison to the tubulin signal, as previously reported (Figure 1P, Δ = 15 nm +/- 8; 22 nm +/- 5; 27 nm +/- 6 and 28 nm +/- 9, respectively) (Le Guennec et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM measurements in Figure 1P and previous work by Le Guennec et al., 2020.

claim: POC16/WDR90 proteins consist of an N-terminal DUF667-containing domain similar to the ciliary inner junction protein FAP20.
source: Proteins of the POC16/WDR90 family consist of an N-terminal DUF667-containing domain (domain of unknown function), similar to the ciliary inner junction protein FAP20 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Yanagisawa et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citation to Yanagisawa et al., 2014.

claim: POC16/WDR90 proteins contain multiple WD40 repeats that form β-propeller structures.
source: followed by multiple WD40 repeats that form β-propeller structures (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Xu and Min, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by structural prediction data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and citation to Xu and Min, 2011.

claim: ptPOC16 is a centriolar component in Paramecium tetraurelia.
source: To this end, we raised an antibody against Paramecium tetraurelia POC16 and confirmed its localization at centrioles similarly to what we found in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and human cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Hamel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The N-terminal part of WDR90 comprising the DUF667 domain (WDR90-N(1-225)) is sufficient to decorate cytoplasmic microtubules when overexpressed in U2OS cells.
source: To do so, we overexpressed the N-terminal part of WDR90 and POC16 comprising the DUF667 domain (WDR90-N(1-225) and POC16(1-295), respectively) fused to GFP in U2OS cells and found that this region is sufficient to decorate cytoplasmic microtubules (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by cell imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: WDR90-N can stabilize microtubules when highly expressed in cells subjected to cold shock treatment.
source: We found that while low expressing cells did not maintain a microtubule network, high expressing cells did. This suggests that WDR90-N can stabilize microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by cold shock experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B-D.

claim: Full-length WDR90 fused to GFP only anecdotally binds microtubules.
source: In contrast, we observed that full-length WDR90 fused to GFP only anecdotally binds microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by cell imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Full-length WDR90 may have an autoinhibition conformation and/or interacting partners preventing microtubule binding in the cytoplasm.
source: This observation suggests a possible autoinhibition conformation of the full-length protein and/or to interacting partners preventing microtubule binding in the cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that full-length WDR90 does not bind microtubules well.

claim: Every POC16/WDR90 DUF667 domain from seven different species directly binds to microtubules in vitro.
source: We found that every POC16/WDR90 DUF667 domain directly binds to microtubules in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by microtubule-pelleting assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Recombinant WDR90-N localizes on in vitro polymerized microtubules as observed by negative staining electron microscopy.
source: This interaction was further confirmed using negative staining electron microscopy, where we could observe recombinant WDR90-N localizing on in vitro polymerized microtubules (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All POC16/WDR90 DUF667 orthologs directly interact with tubulin dimers, generating oligomers that pellet under centrifugation.
source: We observed that all POC16/WDR90 DUF667 orthologs directly interact with tubulin dimers, generating oligomers that pellet under centrifugation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by tubulin-binding assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: WDR90-N pre-complexed with microtubules can simultaneously bind free tubulin, creating an additional level of decoration.
source: We subsequently incubated either WDR90-N or POC16(1-295) pre-complexed with microtubules with an excess of free tubulin and analyzed their structural organization by electron microscopy (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F,G). We observed an additional level of decoration due to the simultaneous binding of the DUF667 domains with tubulin and microtubules (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F,G.

claim: Tubulin-WDR90-N oligomers display an 8.5 nm periodical organization on microtubules.
source: Furthermore, we revealed a 8.5 nm periodical organization of tubulin-WDR90-N oligomers on microtubules (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Monomeric FAP20 interacts with both A- and B-microtubules every 8 nm at the inner junction.
source: similar to the recent high-resolution structure of the ciliary microtubule doublet showing that monomeric FAP20 interacts with both A- and B-microtubules every 8 nm at the inner junction (Khalifa et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Khalifa et al., 2020 and Ma et al., 2019.

claim: POC16/WDR90 is an evolutionary conserved microtubule/tubulin-interacting protein with the capacity to connect microtubules.
source: Based on these results, we concluded that POC16/WDR90 is an evolutionary conserved microtubule/tubulin-interacting protein with the capacity to connect microtubules, a functional prerequisite for an inner junction protein that simultaneously interacts with the A and B microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing microtubule and tubulin binding.

claim: Centrin and HsSAS-6 are recruited early during procentriole formation in S phase.
source: We found that while Centrin and HsSAS-6 are recruited as expected early on during procentriole formation in S phase (22 hr) (Strnad et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3A-F and citation to Strnad et al., 2007.

claim: WDR90 starts appearing on procentrioles in early G2 when procentriole elongation starts.
source: WDR90 starts appearing only in early G2 when procentriole elongation starts (24 hr) (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: WDR90 appears on procentrioles in early G2 and reaches full incorporation by the end of G2.
source: Signal intensity analysis over the cell cycle further demonstrates that WDR90 appears on procentrioles in early G2 and reaches full incorporation by the end of G2 (Figure 3G,H)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity analysis shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: WDR90 incorporation timing is similar to the reported incorporation of the inner scaffold protein POC5.
source: similarly to the reported incorporation of the inner scaffold protein POC5 (Azimzadeh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to previous work cited as Azimzadeh et al., 2009.

claim: WDR90 localizes to centriolar satellites in addition to its centriolar distribution.
source: In addition, we noticed that besides its centriolar distribution, WDR90 localizes also to centriolar satellites, which are macromolecular assemblies of centrosomal proteins scaffolded by the protein PCM1 and involved in centrosomal homeostasis (Drew et al., 2017; Odabasi et al., 2020; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D and citations to Drew et al., 2017 and Odabasi et al., 2020.

claim: WDR90 satellite localization is PCM1-dependent.
source: We found that in absence of PCM1, WDR90 is solely found at centrioles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H), demonstrating that WDR90 satellite localization is PCM1-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by PCM1 depletion experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-H.

claim: WDR90 siRNA-treated cells showed significantly reduced WDR90 levels at centrosomes in comparison to control cells.
source: As previously shown (Hamel et al., 2017), WDR90 siRNA-treated cells showed significantly reduced WDR90 levels at centrosomes in comparison to control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA depletion data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,C and citation to Hamel et al., 2017.

claim: In WDR90-depleted cells, only one of two Centrin-positive centrioles is still associated with WDR90 in G1 and early S-phase (69% compared to 10% in controls).
source: Moreover, we observed an asymmetry in signal reduction at centrioles in WDR90-depleted cells, with only one of two Centrin-positive centrioles still associated with WDR90 in G1 and early S-phase (69% compared to 10% in controls)
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In WDR90-depleted S/G2/M cells, one of four Centrin-positive centrioles retains WDR90 (77% compared to 0% in controls).
source: and one of four Centrin-positive centrioles in S/G2/M cells (77% compared to 0% in controls, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The loss of WDR90 does not result from a duplication failure.
source: As the four Centrin-positive dots indicate duplicated centrioles, this result suggests that the loss of WDR90 does not result from a duplication failure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of four Centrin-positive dots.

claim: The remaining WDR90 signal possibly corresponds to the mother centriole and the daughter has been depleted from WDR90.
source: We postulate therefore that the remaining WDR90 signal possibly corresponds to the mother centriole and that the daughter has been depleted from WDR90 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the asymmetric WDR90 depletion pattern.

claim: WDR90 is stably incorporated into centrioles.
source: We further conclude that WDR90 is stably incorporated into centrioles, in agreement with its possible structural role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the asymmetric depletion pattern and comparison to POC5.

claim: The intensity of the Centrin and POC5 signals were markedly reduced upon WDR90 siRNA treatment.
source: We also noted that the intensity of the Centrin and POC5 signals were markedly reduced upon WDR90 siRNA treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–K).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-K.

claim: Only 39% of WDR90-depleted cells displayed 2 POC5 dots in G1 in contrast to 86% of control cells.
source: Indeed, we found that only 39% of WDR90-depleted cells displayed 2 POC5 dots in G1 (negative for HsSAS-6 signal) in contrast to the 86% of control cells with 2 POC5 dots (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H.

claim: 68% of control cells had 2 to 4 POC5 dots in S/G2/M in contrast to 29% in WDR90-depleted condition.
source: Moreover, 68% of control cells had 2 to 4 POC5 dots in S/G2/M (associated with 2 HsSAS-6 dots) in contrast to 29% in WDR90-depleted condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H.

claim: The HsSAS-6 signal was not affected in WDR90-depleted cells.
source: The HsSAS-6 signal was not affected in WDR90-depleted cells, confirming that initiation of the centriole duplication process is not impaired under this condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G,J,L).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G,J,L.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of the distal centriole cap protein CP110 was not changed under WDR90-depletion.
source: Similarly, the fluorescence intensity of the distal centriole cap protein CP110 was not changed under WDR90-depletion in contrast to the Centrin signal reduction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2M–O).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2M-O.

claim: Expression of GFP-WDR90RR restores partially the Centrin and POC5 signals at centrioles in WDR90-depleted cells.
source: We found that expression of GFP-WDR90RR restores partially the Centrin and POC5 signals at centrioles (Figure 3I–L).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3I-L.

claim: The depletion of WDR90 leads to a decrease in Centrin and POC5 localization at centrioles.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the depletion of WDR90 leads to a decrease in Centrin and POC5 localization at centrioles but does not affect the initiation of centriole duplication nor the recruitment of the distal cap protein CP110.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: WDR90 depletion does not affect the initiation of centriole duplication.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the depletion of WDR90 leads to a decrease in Centrin and POC5 localization at centrioles but does not affect the initiation of centriole duplication nor the recruitment of the distal cap protein CP110.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on HsSAS-6 data.

claim: WDR90 depletion does not affect the recruitment of the distal cap protein CP110.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the depletion of WDR90 leads to a decrease in Centrin and POC5 localization at centrioles but does not affect the initiation of centriole duplication nor the recruitment of the distal cap protein CP110.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on CP110 data.

claim: WDR90-depleted centrioles exhibited a slight tubulin length increase (502 nm +/- 65 compared to 434 nm +/- 58 in controls).
source: Unexpectedly, we found that WDR90-depleted centrioles exhibited a slight tubulin length increase (502 nm +/- 65 compared to 434 nm +/- 58 in controls), potentially indicative of a defect in centriole length regulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM length measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: WDR90-depleted centrioles show a slight decrease in diameter at the level of the central core.
source: In contrast, despite a slight decrease at the level of the central core, we did not observe, in neither of the conditions, any significant difference in centriole diameter at the proximal and very distal regions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by diameter measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The localization of POC1B, FAM161A, POC5 and Centrin in the central core region of centrioles was markedly altered in WDR90-depleted daughter centrioles.
source: We found that the localization of these four proteins in the central core region of centrioles was markedly altered in WDR90-depleted daughter centrioles (Figure 4E,F) using CEP164 to label the mother centriole (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: In WDR90-depleted centrioles, inner scaffold components cover only ~20% of the centriolar lumen at the proximal extremity instead of ~60%.
source: Instead of covering ~60% of the entire centriolar lumen, we only observed a ~ 20% remaining belt, positive for inner scaffold components at the proximal extremity of the core region (Figure 4E–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: This is supported by length coverage measurements shown in Figure 4E-G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Centrin was affected specifically in its inner core distribution upon WDR90 depletion.
source: It should also be noted that Centrin, which displays a central core and an additional distal tip decoration (Le Guennec et al., 2020), was affected specifically in its inner core distribution (Figure 4E white arrow, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E, and citation to Le Guennec et al., 2020.

claim: Upon WDR90 depletion, 10% of cells had their centriolar microtubule wall broken (15 out of 150 centrioles).
source: In line with this hypothesis, we found that upon WDR90 depletion, 10% of cells had their centriolar microtubule wall broken, indicative of microtubule triplets fracture and loss of centriole integrity (15 out of 150 centrioles, Figure 5, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The break in WDR90-depleted centrioles occurred mainly above the remaining belt of inner scaffold components.
source: The break occurred mainly above the remaining belt of inner scaffold components (Figure 5A–D), possibly reflecting a weakened microtubule wall in the central and distal region of the centriole.
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The perfect cylindrical shape (roundness) of the centriolar microtubule wall was affected in WDR90-depleted centrioles with 95% of depleted centrioles in top view affected.
source: We also noticed that the perfect cylindrical shape (defined as roundness) of the centriolar microtubule wall was affected with clear ovoid-shaped or opened centrioles seen from near-perfect top view oriented centrioles (Figure 5E,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, 95% of depleted centrioles in top view are affected)
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 5E,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CEP135 distribution was not altered in WDR90-depleted cells.
source: While CEP135 and glutamylation were not altered in WDR90-depleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–K)
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-K.

claim: Glutamylation (PolyE) was not altered in WDR90-depleted cells.
source: While CEP135 and glutamylation were not altered in WDR90-depleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–K)
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-K.

claim: FOP1 distribution was slightly disturbed at centrioles in WDR90-depleted cells but still present.
source: we found that FOP1 distribution was slightly disturbed at centrioles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L–N) but still present
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1L-N.

claim: POC5 depletion led to a slight centriole elongation.
source: Consistently with WDR90 depletion, we found that the removal of the inner scaffold POC5, which occurs mainly at daughter centrioles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), led to a slight centriole elongation (Figure 6C,D)
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM length measurements shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: POC5 depletion resulted in 10% of broken centrioles (4 out of 46 centrioles).
source: and resulted in 10% of broken centrioles (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B; 4 out of 46 centrioles).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: POC5 depletion leads to shorter procentrioles in metaphase.
source: We also confirmed that POC5 depletion leads to shorter procentrioles in metaphase as previously reported (Azimzadeh et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C and citation to Azimzadeh et al., 2009.

claim: POC5-depleted procentrioles become over elongated just after mitosis.
source: but then become over elongated just after mitosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: WDR90 localization is not affected at centrioles upon POC5 depletion.
source: however, we found this not to be the case, as WDR90 localization is not affected at centrioles upon POC5 depletion (Figure 6E–H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 6E-H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: WDR90 is upstream of POC5.
source: This result therefore indicates that WDR90 is upstream of POC5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that POC5 depletion does not affect WDR90 localization.

claim: The double siRNA depletion of WDR90 and POC5 led to a strong decrease of cell number as compared to WDR90 depletion alone.
source: We found that the double siRNA led to a strong decrease of cell number as compared to WDR90 depletion alone, suggesting either an increase of cell mortality or a defect in cell cycle progression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The remaining POC5 belt found in WDR90-depleted centrioles was completely removed in WDR90/POC5 co-depleted cells.
source: As expected, we found that the remaining POC5 belt found in WDR90-depleted centrioles was completely removed (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Centrioles appeared even further elongated under WDR90/POC5 co-depletion conditions.
source: Moreover, centrioles appeared even further elongated under these conditions, indicating that the complete removal of POC5 further enhances the WDR90 phenotype (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM length measurements shown in Figure 6I,J.

claim: About 30% of centrioles were abnormal in WDR90/POC5 depleted cells (70 out of 260 centrioles).
source: Structurally, we noticed beside the elongated centrioles about 30%, of abnormal centrioles in WDR90/POC5 depleted cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,C,D; 70 out of 260 centrioles)
evidence: This is supported by U-ExM imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,C,D.

claim: WDR90 is crucial to ensure inner core protein localization within the centriole core.
source: Collectively, we demonstrate that WDR90 is crucial to ensure inner core protein localization within the centriole core, as well as to maintain the microtubule wall integrity and the overall centriole roundness and stability (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: WDR90 is crucial to maintain the microtubule wall integrity.
source: Collectively, we demonstrate that WDR90 is crucial to ensure inner core protein localization within the centriole core, as well as to maintain the microtubule wall integrity and the overall centriole roundness and stability (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: WDR90 is crucial to maintain the overall centriole roundness and stability.
source: Collectively, we demonstrate that WDR90 is crucial to ensure inner core protein localization within the centriole core, as well as to maintain the microtubule wall integrity and the overall centriole roundness and stability (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: POC16/WDR90 family proteins constitute an evolutionary conserved central core microtubule triplet component.
source: Our work demonstrates that POC16/WDR90 family proteins constitute an evolutionary conserved central core microtubule triplet component that is essential for maintaining the inner centriolar scaffold components in human centrioles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations across species.

claim: POC16/WDR90 is essential for maintaining the inner centriolar scaffold components in human centrioles.
source: Our work demonstrates that POC16/WDR90 family proteins constitute an evolutionary conserved central core microtubule triplet component that is essential for maintaining the inner centriolar scaffold components in human centrioles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on WDR90 depletion experiments.

claim: The depletion of WDR90 leads to centriolar defects and impairment of microtubule triplets organization resulting in the loss of the canonical circular shape of centrioles.
source: The depletion of WDR90 leads to centriolar defects and impairment of microtubule triplets organization resulting in the loss of the canonical circular shape of centrioles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on U-ExM imaging data.

claim: The overall destabilization of the centriole can lead to microtubule triplet breakage.
source: We also found that this overall destabilization of the centriole can lead to microtubule triplet breakage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on U-ExM imaging data showing broken centrioles.

claim: POC16/WDR90 localizes at the inner junction of the A and B microtubule of the centriolar microtubule triplet.
source: In addition and based on the sequence and structural similarity to the DUF667 domain of FAP20 that composes the inner junction in flagella, we propose that POC16/WDR90 localizes at the inner junction of the A and B microtubule of the centriolar microtubule triplet.
evidence: This is a proposal based on sequence similarity and structural modeling.

claim: Another protein, possibly FAP20, could mediate the inner junction between A- and B-microtubule in the proximal region of the centriole.
source: The fact that WDR90 localization is restricted to the central core region led us to hypothesize that another protein, possibly FAP20 as it has been previously reported at centrioles (Yanagisawa et al., 2014), could mediate the inner junction between A- and B-microtubule in the proximal region of the centriole.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the restricted localization of WDR90 and citation to Yanagisawa et al., 2014.

claim: The WD40 domains of POC16/WDR90 might be located inside the B-microtubule of the triplet.
source: Moreover, in POC16/WDR90 proteins, the DUF667 domain is followed by a WD40 domain sharing a similarity with the flagellar inner B-microtubule protein FAP52/WDR16 (Owa et al., 2019) leading us to propose that the WD40 domains of POC16/WDR90 might also be located inside the B-microtubule of the triplet.
evidence: This is a proposal based on sequence similarity to FAP52/WDR16 and citation to Owa et al., 2019.

claim: FAM161A is a microtubule-binding protein close to the inner microtubule wall of the centriole.
source: Indeed, we and others also previously show that FAM161A (Le Guennec et al., 2020; Zach et al., 2012), similarly to WDR90, is a microtubule-binding protein close to the inner microtubule wall of the centriole
evidence: This is supported by citations to Le Guennec et al., 2020 and Zach et al., 2012.

claim: Both WDR90 and FAM161A might compose the stem and link the microtubule triplets to the inner scaffold.
source: raising the possibility that both might compose the stem and link the microtubule triplets to the inner scaffold.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the similar properties of WDR90 and FAM161A.

claim: WDR90 is recruited to centrioles in G2 phase of the cell cycle concomitant with centriole elongation and inner central core assembly.
source: Our work further establishes that WDR90 is recruited to centrioles in G2 phase of the cell cycle concomitant with centriole elongation and inner central core assembly.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on cell cycle analysis data.

claim: WDR90 depletion does not impair centriole duplication nor microtubule wall assembly.
source: We found that WDR90 depletion does not impair centriole duplication nor microtubule wall assembly, as noted by the presence of the proximal marker HsSAS-6 and the distal cap CP110.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on HsSAS-6 and CP110 data.

claim: WDR90 depletion leads to a strong reduction of inner scaffold components at centrioles.
source: In stark contrast, WDR90 depletion leads to a strong reduction of inner scaffold components at centrioles, as well as some centriole destabilization.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on U-ExM imaging data.

claim: Delta- and Epsilon-tubulin mutants affect centriole integrity in several model organisms.
source: For instance, Delta- and Epsilon-tubulin mutants have been shown in several model organisms to affect centriole integrity (Dutcher et al., 2002; Dutcher and Trabuco, 1998; Garreau de Loubresse et al., 2001; O'Toole et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Delta- and Epsilon-tubulin null mutant human cells lack microtubule triplets and have unstable centrioles that do not persist to the next cell cycle.
source: with notably in human cells where Delta- and Epsilon-tubulin null mutant cells were shown to lack microtubule triplets and have thus unstable centrioles that do not persist to the next cell cycle (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Delta- and Epsilon-tubulin null mutant centrioles can elongate with proper recruitment of HsSAS-6 and CP110 but fail to recruit POC5.
source: Remarkably, these centrioles can elongate with a proper recruitment of the cartwheel component HsSAS-6 and the distal marker CP110 but fails to recruit POC5, a result that is similar to our findings with WDR90-depleted cells.
evidence: This is a comparison to the authors' findings, drawing on the citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: WDR90 might not be recruited in Delta- and Epsilon-tubulin null mutant centrioles because the A- and B-microtubule inner junction would be missing.
source: As Delta- and Epsilon-tubulin null human mutant cells can solely assemble microtubule singlets (Wang et al., 2017), we speculate that WDR90 might not be recruited in these centrioles, as the A- and B-microtubule inner junction would be missing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the authors' model and citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: WDR90 as well as POC5 depletion affects centriole length in human cells.
source: Our work also showed that WDR90 as well as POC5 depletion affects centriole length in human cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on U-ExM length measurements.

claim: WDR90 and POC5 have a role in overall centriole length regulation.
source: Altogether, these results emphasize the role of these two proteins in overall centriole length regulation and suggest an unexpected role of the inner scaffold structure in centriole length control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed length changes upon depletion.

claim: The inner scaffold structure has an unexpected role in centriole length control.
source: Altogether, these results emphasize the role of these two proteins in overall centriole length regulation and suggest an unexpected role of the inner scaffold structure in centriole length control.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the length phenotype.

claim: The concomitant elongation of the centriole with the appearance of inner scaffold components in G2 can act on the final length of this organelle.
source: It is very likely that the concomitant elongation of the centriole with the appearance of inner scaffold components in G2 can act on the final length of this organelle.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the timing of WDR90 recruitment and length phenotype.
